title: A Song Junk Lifted in a Steel Cage
place: Maritime Silk Road Museum, Hailing Island, Yangjiang, Guangdong, China
text: In 1987 a British firm hunting a Dutch wreck off Guangdong found a 100-foot Southern Song junk instead. For two decades the Chinese Navy kept fishermen away with tales of live wartime bombs. In 2007 a 3,000-ton steel cage scooped up the ship with its sediment, 15,600 tons in all. An ink inscription links its building to 1183, and it holds 60,000 to 80,000 objects.

source.name: National Geographic: China kept this 800-year-old shipwreck a secret for decades

title: Cargo Tagged for a Kyoto Temple
place: Off Sinan, between Jeungdo and Imjado, South Jeolla, South Korea
text: In 1975 a fisherman off Korea's southwest coast found a piece of pottery caught in his net. Divers then spent until 1984 excavating a merchant ship that left Ningbo for Japan around the sixth month of 1323. It held over 22,000 catalogued objects and about 28 tons of Chinese copper coins. Of 364 wooden shipping tags, 41 name Tofukuji, a Kyoto temple.

source.name: International Journal of Korean Art and Archaeology: Sinan Shipwreck Collection at the National Museum of Korea

title: The Fleet the Divine Wind Sank
place: Off Takashima Island, Matsuura, Nagasaki, Japan
text: In 1281 Kublai Khan sent some 4,400 ships carrying at least 140,000 Korean, Mongol and Chinese troops to invade Japan. A two-day typhoon, remembered as the kamikaze or 'divine wind', apparently wrecked about 80 percent of them. In 2011 archaeologists off Takashima found a ship believed to be from that fleet, under 25 metres of water and a metre of sand, with over 4,000 artifacts.

source.name: The Conversation: The original kamikaze: Kublai Khan's invasion shipwreck found?

title: Saved by a Lighthouse Beam
place: Kashinozaki, Kii Oshima, Kushimoto, Wakayama, Japan
text: The Ottoman frigate Ertugrul came to Japan on a goodwill visit with over 600 men. Heading home on 16 September 1890, it broke up on rocks off Kii Oshima in a typhoon, and 587 died. Sixty-nine survivors followed the Kashinozaki lighthouse beam, some climbing a 40-metre cliff, and islanders shared scarce food. In 1985 Turkey flew 215 Japanese out of Tehran, citing that old debt.

source.name: Nippon.com: The Sinking of the Ertugrul: Japan and Turkey Mark the 125th Anniversary of the Tragedy

title: A Sewn Ship Full of Tang Bowls
place: Batu Hitam reef, off Belitung Island, Indonesia
text: Around the 830s, an 18-metre ship sewn together in Persian Gulf style sank off Sumatra after loading cargo in southern China. It lay untouched until found by chance in 1998. Inside were more than 50,000 hand-painted bowls from Changsha in Hunan, fine celadons, early blue-and-white dishes, and a gold cup from Yangzhou with Central Asian musicians, the largest of its type known.

source.name: Asian Civilisations Museum: Tang Shipwreck

title: Singapore's First Ancient Shipwreck
place: Eastern entrance of the Singapore Strait, Singapore
text: No ancient wreck had ever been found in Singapore's waters until the Temasek Wreck. Lead researcher Michael Flecker thinks it was a Chinese junk that sailed from Quanzhou between 1340 and 1352, when Temasek, the port before Singapore, was a busy hub. Divers raised about 3.8 tons of ceramics, including pieces of around 300 Yuan blue-and-white bowls, more than any other documented shipwreck.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Singapore's First Ancient Shipwreck Reveals Cargo of Yuan Dynasty Porcelain

title: A Scuttled Submarine in the Strait
place: Strait of Malacca, off Malaysia and Thailand
text: During the Second World War, the US submarine Grenadier was bombed by a Japanese plane in the Strait of Malacca. All 76 crew survived, scuttled their boat and were held prisoner for more than two years; four died from harsh treatment. In 2020 divers said they believed they had found the wreck. Diver Lance Horowitz said its measurements match the submarine's naval records.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: World War II-Era Sub Spotted in Southeast Asian Waters

title: A Silk Road Wreck Off Sri Lanka
place: Off Godavaya, Hambantota District, Sri Lanka
text: Off Sri Lanka's southern coast, near the fishing village of Godavaya, lies a ship about 2,000 years old. Strong Indian Ocean currents have left only a concreted mound of timber scraps, glass ingots, corroded iron and copper ingots, grinding stones and pottery. German archaeologists had found a second-century CE port nearby, a stop on the maritime Silk Road, so its goods may have been bound for Rome.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Shipwreck May Offer Clues to Ancient East-West Trade

title: Da Gama's Uncle Ignores a Storm
place: Al Hallaniyah, Khuriya Muriya Islands, Oman
text: In 1503 Vicente Sodré, Vasco da Gama's uncle, left his post guarding India's coast to loot Arab ships. Anchored off Al Hallaniyah, his squadron ignored local warnings of a storm, and the Esmeralda went down with its crew. Divers have recovered about 2,800 artifacts, including a bell that may read 1498, believed to be the oldest ship's bell found, and a rare silver coin minted for India trade.

source.name: National Geographic: Shipwreck Discovered from Explorer Vasco da Gama's Fleet

title: A Stone Age Wall Against the Sea
place: Tel Hreiz, Carmel coast, Israel
text: Off Israel's Carmel coast, a drowned farming village holds what researchers call the oldest known coastal defence. Some 7,000 years ago villagers dragged boulders weighing up to a tonne into a wall over 100 metres long to hold back the waves. Hundreds of waterlogged olive pits hint they made oil. But the sea kept rising, 4 to 7 mm a year, and the village was finally swamped.

source.name: PLOS ONE: A submerged 7000-year-old village and seawall demonstrate earliest known coastal defence against sea-level rise

title: An Ancient Town Under a Reservoir
place: Hasankeyf, Batman Province, Turkey
text: Hasankeyf, carved into a plateau above the Tigris, had been lived in for some 12,000 years, overlooked by caves cut by Neolithic settlers. Then came Turkey's Ilisu Dam. Residents were told to leave by 8 October 2019, and the reservoir was expected to drown about 80 percent of the town, displacing some 3,000 people. Its minaret and some artifacts were to be moved to safer ground.

source.name: National Geographic: In Turkey, a power play will leave ancient towns underwater

title: The Wreck That Taught Archaeologists to Dive
place: Yassiada islet, near Bodrum, Turkey
text: In summer 626 CE, during the last great war of antiquity, a 60-ton Byzantine ship carrying about 800 amphorae of wine and oil for the troops sank off a rocky islet near Bodrum. From 1961 George Bass's team dived about 120 feet down, pinning hull scraps with sharpened bicycle spokes and tagging finds with cut linoleum, proving archaeology could be done properly underwater.

source.name: National Geographic: This shipwreck off Bodrum transformed underwater archaeology

title: The Slave Ship Wrecked off Cape Town
place: Off Clifton, Cape Town, South Africa
text: In December 1794 the Portuguese ship São José sailed from Mozambique for Brazil with more than 400 enslaved people aboard. Rough seas drove it onto rocks off Cape Town. More than 200 captives died in the waves, and about 300 survivors were sold into slavery in Cape Town. Forgotten for two centuries, it became the first wreck known to have sunk with captive Africans aboard to be found.

source.name: Iziko Museums of South Africa: Unshackled History: The Wreck of the Slave Ship, São José, 1794

source2.name: NOAA Office of National Marine Sanctuaries: Connecting Ancestral Memory Through the São José Paquete de Africa and the Clotilda

title: Treasure Ship in the Diamond Desert
place: Sperrgebiet, north of the Orange River mouth, Namibia
text: In April 2008 a geologist in a Namibian diamond mine picked a copper ingot out of the sand. It came from the Bom Jesus, a Portuguese ship that left Lisbon in 1533 and vanished in a storm. Archaeologists uncovered 22 tons of copper ingots, more than 2,000 gold coins and elephant tusks. Toe bones inside a shoe were the only human remains found.

source.name: National Geographic: Shipwreck in the Forbidden Zone

title: Da Gama's Last Fleet off Kenya
place: Off Malindi, Kilifi County, Kenya
text: Found in 2013 about 20 feet down and 1,600 feet from Malindi's shore, this wreck may be the São Jorge, one of some 20 ships in Vasco da Gama's final fleet, known to have sunk in 1524. Divers from the National Museum of Kenya recovered hull timbers, copper ingots and elephant tusks. A survey of 15 miles of coral reef helped researchers support the identification.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Mystery Shipwreck Off Coast of Kenya Confirmed to Be Part of Vasco da Gama's Final Voyage

title: A Viceroy's Ship Taken by Pirates
place: Nosy Boraha (Île Sainte-Marie), Madagascar
text: In 1721 the Portuguese ship Nossa Senhora do Cabo left India for Portugal carrying gold, silver, gems, the outgoing viceroy and the Archbishop of Goa. Off Madagascar, pirates led by Olivier Levasseur, known as La Buse, and John Taylor captured it. Divers near Nosy Boraha, once the pirate haunt of Île Sainte-Marie, have recovered more than 3,300 artifacts, including religious objects made in Goa.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Divers Discover Portuguese Shipwreck Off Madagascar

title: Statues Rise From Drowned Canopus
place: Abu Qir Bay, near Alexandria, Egypt
text: In August 2025 cranes lifted three statues out of Egypt's Abu Qir Bay: a quartzite sphinx bearing Ramesses II's cartouche, a granite colossus from the late Ptolemaic era and a marble Roman nobleman. They came from a 2,000-year-old settlement, probably part of Canopus, that earthquakes and rising seas pushed under the Mediterranean. Divers also mapped temples, houses and a 400-foot dock.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Statues from Sunken Egyptian City Reemerge

title: The Last Slave Ship, Burned and Sunk
place: Mobile River, near Africatown, Mobile, Alabama, USA
text: On 9 July 1860 the Clotilda sailed into Mobile Bay with 110 captives from present-day Benin, the last known slave ship to reach the United States. To destroy the evidence, Timothy Meaher and Captain William Foster burned, sank and abandoned it. The survivors built a new home now called Africatown. The wreck was found in the Mobile River and confirmed in 2019.

source.name: Alabama Historical Commission: Clotilda

source2.name: NOAA Office of National Marine Sanctuaries: Connecting Ancestral Memory Through the São José Paquete de Africa and the Clotilda

title: La Salle's Last Ship in Texas Mud
place: Matagorda Bay, Texas, USA
text: In 1684 Louis XIV sent La Salle with four ships and about 400 people to settle near the Mississippi's mouth. He overshot, lost ships to pirates and disaster, and was killed by his own men. La Belle, the last ship, sank in a 1686 storm in Matagorda Bay. Found in 1995, it yielded over 1.8 million artifacts, including 785,000 glass beads and 600 muskets.

source.name: Bullock Texas State History Museum: La Belle

title: The Ironclad Lost on New Year's Eve
place: Off Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, USA
text: The Civil War ironclad USS Monitor was under tow by the Rhode Island when a storm struck off Cape Hatteras on 31 December 1862. Leaks flooded the engine room, the crew raised a red distress lantern, and men crossing the deck to the turret were swept away. Sixteen died. Found in 1973 under about 230 feet of water, the wreck became the first US national marine sanctuary.

source.name: NOAA Monitor National Marine Sanctuary: History of USS Monitor

source2.name: NOAA Monitor National Marine Sanctuary: Discovery and Designation

title: Two and a Half Miles Down
place: North Atlantic, about 350 nautical miles off Newfoundland, Canada
text: In April 1912, five days out of Southampton, RMS Titanic struck an iceberg, broke apart and sank. More than 1,500 passengers and crew died. The wreck stayed hidden until 1 September 1985, when a joint American-French expedition found it about 12,500 feet down. In 1986 a plaque was placed on the wreck asking that it be left undisturbed in memory of those lost.

source.name: NOAA Office of General Counsel: R.M.S. Titanic, History and Significance

title: Mutiny on a Shipwreck Island
place: Morning Reef, Beacon Island, Houtman Abrolhos, Western Australia, Australia
text: On 4 June 1629 the Dutch East India Company ship Batavia struck a reef near Beacon Island in the Houtman Abrolhos. Of the 322 aboard, 40 drowned and the rest got ashore. Commander Francisco Pelsaert sailed to Batavia for help, and while he was gone Jeronimus Cornelisz led a murderous mutiny among the stranded survivors. Divers salvaged cannon, an anchor and stern timbers in 1970 to 1974.

source.name: Western Australian Museum: Batavia (Maritime Archaeology Database)

title: Australia's Oldest Known Shipwreck
place: Trial Rocks, off north-west Western Australia, Australia
text: In May 1622 the English East Indiaman Trial, bound from Plymouth to Batavia, struck rocks off north-west Australia at night. Commander John Brooke escaped in a small skiff with his son and nine others, while Thomas Bright and 35 more took the longboat; about 93 sailors were lost. Divers found the likely site in 1969, and it is Australia's oldest known shipwreck.

source.name: Western Australian Museum: Trial (Maritime Archaeology Database)

title: Stone Tools on the Drowned Shelf
place: Cape Bruguieres Channel, Murujuga (Dampier Archipelago), Western Australia, Australia
text: At the height of the last Ice Age, the sea stood about 130 metres lower and Australia was a third larger. Off Murujuga, divers found 269 stone artefacts in the Cape Bruguieres Channel, about 190 permanently underwater and at least 7,000 years old, plus a tool 14 metres down beside a drowned freshwater spring. They are Australia's first confirmed ancient underwater sites on the continental shelf.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Aboriginal artefacts on the continental shelf reveal ancient drowned cultural landscapes in northwest Australia

title: Streets Beneath the Greek Sea
place: Pavlopetri, Laconia, Greece
text: Off southern Greece lie the streets of Pavlopetri, settled by around 3500 BCE and later a trading centre of Mycenaean Greece. Three main roads linked some 50 rectangular buildings, each with an open courtyard, and Minoan-style loom weights hint at weaving. Earthquakes, tsunamis and rising seas submerged it more than 3,000 years ago. Nicholas Flemming discovered it in 1967.

source.name: National Geographic: These ancient cities sunk to the ocean floor. Here's how they were rediscovered.
